newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah stable, shrugs off trade data.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah stable, shrugs off trade data.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah was stable against the dollar in slow late trading on Wednesday, shrugging off a sharp drop in the March trade surplus, dealers said.
They said the rupiah seemed to perform well and withstood the sharp fall in the March trade surplus although it was briefly jolted by a bomb scare at the Japanese embassy.

One U.S. bank dealer said news of a bomb threat at the Japanese embassy did briefly cause some dollar purchases, but strong rupiah support after a relatively smooth election seemed to outweigh any negative news at the moment.
The embassy on Wednesday received a second telephoned hoax bomb threat in eight days. No explosives were found.
One Japanese bank dealer said London investment houses were seen establishing fresh long rupiah positions after the polls.
"Sentiment on the rupiah is so good that negative news have little impact on it. We expect the rupiah to test the 2,425.0 level in the short-term," the Japanese bank dealer said.
Spot rupiah was at 2,427.5/28.0 at 0915 GMT after rising to a high of 2,426.5 from an opening of 2,427.0/28.0. Dealers said trading was trapped in a narrow range between 2,426 and 2,428.
Tomorrow and today rupiah closed at 2,427.50/27.75 and 2,426.0/26.5, respectively.

Dealers said a mixed set of macro economic figure had not had any negative impact on the rupiah. Instead, operators were looking for higher rupiah levels closing to the lower end of the central bank's intervention band.
Economists said Indonesia's economic fundamentals were fairly favourable compared with other countries in the region and they were not overly concerned about short-term volatility.
The trade surplus fell to $243.3 million in March from $964.3 million in February while the May year-on-year inflation was contained at 5.08 percent against 4.95 percent in April.
Some said the sharp drop in the trade surplus was due to softer oil prices in March. They expressed concern over increased consumer demand due to declining interest rates.

"In terms of oil exports, they have dropped 1.7 percent year-on-year. That was probably due to the lower oil prices for the month of March," Ng Bock Eng, economist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore, said.
"I think if you take a broader perspective rather than just month-to-month changes, they are still fairly good numbers, compared to the region, for example," he said.
The Japanese bank dealer said ample rupiah liquidity in the afternoon did not reverse early rises of longer-term swaps.
Overnight money fell to five percent from 12.0 percent in the morning. But longer-term swap rates were steady, suggesting offshore players were extending long forward positions.
Overnight swap was at 0.35/0.45 and tom/next at par/0.1.
One-month swaps were at 12.25/13.00, two at 25.25/26.25, three at 38.5/39.5 and six at 77.0/79.0 points.
The central bank kept its intervention band at 2,418/2,610 and its conversion band at 2,418/2,466 on Wednesday.
Dealers said the market focus was also on a meeting due to be held on Thursday of the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) to decide whether the party will accept the election outcome.
The PPP has claimed there were widespread irregularities before and during the May 29 poll.
The ruling Golkar party won a record 74 percent of the national vote, with the PPP taking nearly 23 percent.
Many analysts remained cautious over possible post-election violence if the PPP refused to sign the election result.
